newsitem.title: HAITI: Aristide recalls coup against him five years ago.
newsitem.headline: Aristide recalls coup against him five years ago.

text.p: Former President Jean-Bertrand Aristide remembers Sept. 30, 1991, as one of the saddest days he has seen in this impoverished Caribbean nation.
Responding to a rumor that Haiti's military was about to launch a coup, Aristide marched to the National Palace surrounded by supporters in a failed attempt to stop the overthrow of his government.

"It was a sad time, but it was also beautiful to see how the people united," he recalled. "When (coup leader Gen. Raoul) Cedras' people started shooting, I went outside. They were afraid to see me coming."

Aristide, having survived multiple assassination attempts, said the gunfire did not faze him. "I was used to it," he said, laughing. "They tried to kill me nine times. But then I had to think of protecting the people that were with us."

Aristide was forced into exile, while an estimated 5,000 Haitians were killed during three years of brutal military rule. Tens of thousands of others were raped, beaten, tortured, forced into hiding or forced to risk boarding rickety boats bound for the United States.

Aristide -- interviewed in his office at his sprawling estate just outside Port-au-Prince on Thursday -- has seen a vast improvement in his situation in the two years since he was restored to power. The restoration followed the ousting of the junta by a peaceful U.S.-led military intervention in September 1994.
Five years after the coup, Aristide was again bound for the United States. This time, though, it was for a speaking tour and a world leaders' conference in San Francisco.

Late in his presidency, the former Roman Catholic priest who rose to power on a wave of popular support, becoming Haiti's first freely elected president in 1991, married lawyer Mildred Trouillot. She is expecting their first child next month.

By all accounts, Aristide is likely to be a formidable contender for president in 2000. He steadfastly declines comment on his political plans, but even as he left office in February, signs around the capital urged him to run again.

Aristide, a small man speaking softly from behind his desk, said that on balance, Haiti was also far better off now than during the coup years. "The main difference now is that there is no army," he said.
Aristide disbanded the military soon after his return, but he now criticizes the United States and others involved in the Haiti peacekeeping mission for failing to disarm the populace.
"Before we came back, we said the success of the operation depends on total disarmament," he said. "But instead we have a heavily armed group of angry ex-soldiers."

In late August, a group suspected of being composed of former soldiers attacked the Port-au-Prince police station and parliament building. A day later, two members of an opposition party linked to the former military were killed.

Aristide said he did not believe U.S. State Department allegations that President Rene Preval's private security force was behind the double assassination, which some believed to be retaliation for the attacks of the night before.
Currently about two dozen U.S. diplomatic security agents guard the palace, apparently to maintain order while Preval opens a probe into whether his security force was involved.
"I don't believe they did it," Aristide said. "There are so many thugs and internal conflicts."

While he did not comment on whether he thought Preval made a mistake by allowing the U.S. diplomatic security team into his house, Aristide made some tacit criticism of Preval's performance as president. Preval has come under fire from human rights groups frustrated with the low priority given to prosecution of coup-era crimes.
"I believe justice will be done only because I believe the Haitian people are watching, and if it is not done, they will move to speed the process," he said.
Aristide also has spoken out against privatization of publicly owned enterprises like the electric and phone companies, which Preval has championed.

But despite his differences with Preval, Aristide said they remained close friends, and he likened the political movement to which they both belong to a family that has internal conflict but sticks together.
